To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
there is significant excess familial clustering in the Utah population for cancers of the lip, chronic lymphatic leukemia (CLL), thyroid, lung, and prostate.
the Utah Population Database has provided significant evidence for a genetic contribution to risk for lip, chronic lymphoid leukemia, thyroid, prostate, lung, and melanoma cancers.
we have identified 6 new cancer sites that have a heritable component to their familial clustering.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the genetic and environmental contributions to cancer risk.
the identification of cancer risk factors and their interactions with other diseases.
the identification of the genetic and environmental factors that influence cancer risk, and the application of that knowledge to cancer control and prevention.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there are no common cancers that do not have a genetic basis.
a genetic contribution exists for all cancer sites, and the magnitude of this contribution is variable and site specific.
there is a significant contribution of heritable factors to the familial clustering of risk for cancer at 12 sites, including lip, thyroid, chronic lymphocid leukemia, lung, prostate and melanoma.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

there is significant evidence for a genetic component to cancer risk for 18 of the 26 cancer sites that we have tested, and that the remaining 8 sites are not significantly different from the expected familial clustering that would be due to environmental and non-genetic familial factors alone.
a heritable component exists in cancer risk for 20 of 26 sites tested.
the familiality of cancer is more extensive than previously appreciated.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is more familial clustering than we previously thought for many cancer sites.
cancer risk is a complex phenomenon, and that genetic factors are likely to be important for a larger fraction of cancer sites than previously thought.
there is significant evidence for heritable contributions to cancer risk for a large number of cancer sites, including several new cancer sites.
